articles.title: China's export controls on PV: Precision, balance, and rules-based - CGTN
articles.summary: China's export controls on PV: Precision, balance, and rules-based  CGTN
articles.full_text:

Wind and solar power facilities in Tongxin, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region,China, Oct 14, 2026. /VCG
Editor's note: Xu Xiaohua is chairman of Anhui Huasun Energy Co., Ltd., vice chairman of the Finance Committee, co-chair of the Perovskite Committee of the China Photovoltaic Industry Association, and chairman of the Supervisory Board of the Anhui New Energy Chamber of Commerce. The article reflects the author's opinions and not necessarily the views of CGTN.
Recently, relevant Chinese authorities have introduced specific measures governing export controls on photovoltaic (PV) cell manufacturing equipment and technology. In light of industry practice, several observations are worth sharing.
Controls aim to safeguard China's competitive advantage in the global PV industry
Over more than two decades, China's PV sector has built a fully integrated industrial chain spanning polysilicon, wafers, cells, modules, and core manufacturing equipment, securing a pivotal position in global markets. This hard-won advantage is the fruit of relentless effort, sustained investment, and continuous innovation by generations of PV pioneers. It also serves as a critical pillar for maintaining China's manufacturing competitiveness in the global energy transition.
The global PV industry is at a critical juncture, defined by accelerating technology iteration and intensifying market competition. As the key vehicle for core process technology, PV manufacturing equipment embodies China's accumulated mass-production experience and industrial scale-up expertise. Imposing necessary controls on cutting-edge core equipment that represents next-generation PV technology can help prevent the unwarranted transfer of critical technology and process know-how, safeguarding China's global competitive edge and long-term development potential in the PV industry. This policy arrangement enables China to retain strategic initiative in global PV technology competition. In essence, it is a legitimate measure to safeguard national strategic interests and preserve the industry's long-term competitiveness.
View of a photovoltaic power station on mountains, Rizhao City, Shandong Province, China, Oct 13, 2026. /VCG
Controls demonstrate a measured and rational governance philosophy
The policy follows a category-based, targeted management philosophy. Instead of resorting to simple, blanket restrictions across the board, it applies targeted regulatory controls to relevant equipment based on differences across technology generations. Equipment that has achieved commercial maturity and boasts ample market supply continues to enjoy space for normal international trade, whereas highly sensitive core equipment at the technological frontier is subject to cautious, prudent management.
This institutional framework reflects the principles of pragmatism, targeted policy implementation, and balanced oversight, maintaining a rational, measured stance: It respects industrial reality and focuses on critical segments and core equipment, while also leaving necessary room for mature application and large-scale deployment of related technologies. For PV cell manufacturers, this regulatory approach will not disrupt their routine overseas business expansion. Ultimately, enterprises' international competitiveness hinges on their manufacturing processes, mass-production experience, and capacity for continuous innovation. By maintaining a relatively open approach to mature equipment, the policy underscores a commitment to balancing security and development. Furthermore, it reflects the wisdom, vision, and strategic responsibility of a major power actively participating in and regulating international trade.
A rooftop photovoltaic power generation base in Fangxian County, Hubei Province, China, Oct 13, 2026. /VCG
Policy implementation requires coordination across the entire industry chain
The implementation of export controls on PV equipment is inseparable from coordinated efforts by industry associations, government authorities, cell and module manufacturers, and equipment producers. Enterprises concerned must further strengthen compliance awareness and operate in strict accordance with relevant policy requirements. At the same time, they must also continue to scale up R&D investment and improve their capacity for independent innovation to leverage technological progress to underpin their international competitiveness.
Safeguarded by measured and rational controls, China's PV sector is well-positioned to contribute even greater wisdom and industrial momentum to the global energy transition.

articles.title: China Plans to Tighten Export Controls on AI Technologies - NTD News
articles.summary: China Plans to Tighten Export Controls on AI Technologies  NTD News
articles.full_text:
Beijing is considering adding artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies to its export controls list, aiming to tighten controls on the strategic industry amid rivalry with the United States.
The Chinese Ministry of Commerce unveiled the plan on Oct. 16, covering 40 technologies across three categories Beijing considers important.
The proposed measures identified 23 AI-related technologies subject to export controls, including large AI models, AI agents, AI chip design, computing clusters, voice recognition, high-performance translation, deepfake detection, and hacking-related technologies.
In addition to AI, it listed five biopharmaceutical technologies—such as cell and gene therapies—and 12 photovoltaic technologies, including those used to make polysilicon, a key raw material for solar panels.
“We want to ensure that AI technologies remain safe and controllable,” a spokesperson for the commerce ministry said in a separate statement on Oct. 16.
The ministry said China has simultaneously introduced a temporary registration requirement that covers all the listed technologies.
Starting Oct. 16, exporters must register with the authorities if they plan to transfer intellectual property to overseas entities, grant licenses to foreign companies to use Chinese technology, or transfer ownership of Chinese technology to any foreign party, according to the ministry.
The temporary registration rules also apply to transactions that have already commenced but have not yet been completed, the ministry said.
AI technology already released into the public domain, including through open-source projects or academic papers, will be exempt from the new restrictions, it said.
Certain technologies related to open-source activities and international cooperation may qualify for streamlined licensing procedures, but the decision will depend on the activity and the technology involved, according to the ministry.
The deployment of a restricted AI model on an overseas server or other infrastructure may fall within the scope of the new export controls, Beijing said. However, streamlined licensing procedures may apply if the deployment was to a Chinese company's own overseas cloud infrastructure, or in other “relatively controllable-risk circumstances,” the ministry said.
The move “can be seen as a response to Western countries posting sovereignty requirements on AI, robotics, telecommunications, and other key technologies,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. The aim would be to better regulate access to Chinese technologies, he said.
In the Sept. 8 alert, the FBI, the National Security Agency, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said the Chinese AI companies' practices are “likely with Chinese government awareness.”

articles.title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
articles.summary: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation RegulationUS corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influe...
articles.full_text:
US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.
Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.
US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.
The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.
In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.
Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.
It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.
The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.
Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.
Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.
Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.
The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.
Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”
Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”
US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.
The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”
The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.
The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”
Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

articles.full_text: In this document, the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau (Bureau) invites interested parties to comment on the Upper C-band Transition Preliminary Cost Catalog (Cost Catalog), which is attached as Attachment A. The Cost Catalog contains preliminary estimates of reasonable and necessary transition costs that eligible space station operators and incumbent earth station operators (collectively, incumbents) may incur as they transition out of 4.0-4.16 GHz to make 160 megahertz of mid-band spectrum available to 3.7 GHz Service licensees for flexible use throughout the contiguous United States. The Cost Catalog also includes the payment categories for incumbent earth station operators that elect lump sum reimbursement in lieu of actual cost reimbursement. In Upper C-band (3.98-4.2 GHz); Expanding Flexible Use of the 3.7 to 4.2 GHz Band, GN Docket Nos. 25-59 and 18-122, Report and Order, Order of Proposed Modification, and Order on Reconsideration, FCC 26-46 (July 24, 2026) (Upper C-band R&O), the Commission established that new 3.7 GHz Service licensees will reimburse incumbents for their reasonable and necessary relocation costs to transition out of 4.0-4.16 GHz and directed the Bureau to develop the Cost Catalog.

Take may result from oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities occurring for a period of 5 years. Oil and gas industry operations include similar types of activities covered by the previous 5-year Beaufort Sea incidental take regulations effective from August 6, 2021, through August 5, 2026. We will issue letters of authorization, upon request, for specific activities in accordance with these regulations.

articles.full_text: The National Park Service (NPS) amends its regulations for hunting, fishing, trapping, and other harvest-related activities in Alaska and the procedures used to restrict public use and access in Alaska park areas, including for subsistence. This rule restores the regulatory framework adopted to implement the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980 (ANILCA) in 1981 that guided management for more than three decades, with targeted updates to that framework in response to public comments and further agency review. The restored framework recognizes the complementary and distinct roles of the State of Alaska, the Federal Subsistence Management Program, and the NPS in managing public uses and resources in Alaska park areas. The rule removes regulatory changes made in 2015, 2017, and 2024 that departed from that framework. These amendments are consistent with Executive Orders 14153 and 14192 and Secretary of the Interior's Orders 3422 and 3447.

articles.full_text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is finalizing an approval of a revision to the Arizona State Implementation Plan (SIP) submitted by the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ). This revision includes statutes and regulations amending the Cleaner Burning Gasoline (CBG) program, which is a control measure in the greater Phoenix metropolitan area to reduce emissions of ozone- forming pollutants, carbon monoxide (CO), and particulate matter. Additionally, this revision addresses the Winter Oxygenated Fuel program to control CO emissions in the Tucson area. Finally, this revision repeals the Arizona Gasoline Set[hyphen]aside (GSA) Program, applicable to the 1971 carbon monoxide nonattainment area covering Maricopa County and a portion of Pima County. This SIP revision is administrative in nature. This final action updates the existing SIP- approved CBG program with revisions that have been adopted and implemented by the State to clarify requirements, update references, and enhance flexibility of the program and will not impose any additional costs or regulatory burdens.
